claims.source: Fletcher Vredenburgh, Black Gate, 20 November 2018
claims.quote: a jumbled collection of disparate bits and pieces forced together

claims.claim: Vredenburgh reads the garbled inset tales as a reminder that storytelling is not automatically truthful.
claims.source: Fletcher Vredenburgh, Black Gate, 20 November 2018
claims.quote: storytelling is not automatically truthful

claims.claim: A reader comments that Severian's noting the mountains rising to cover the sun conveyed his worldview without explanation.
claims.source: commenter 'Eugene R.' on Fletcher Vredenburgh, Black Gate, 20 November 2018
claims.quote: how the mountains had risen up to cover the Sun

claims.claim: A reader reports the distancing effect landing when a photograph of Neil Armstrong appears on a library wall as an unknown figure.
claims.source: commenter 'deuce' on Fletcher Vredenburgh, Black Gate, 20 November 2018
claims.quote: there was a photo of Neil Armstrong

claims.claim: Gaiman describes Severian as a perfectly reliable unreliable narrator.
claims.source: Neil Gaiman, 'My hero: Gene Wolfe', The Guardian, 13 May 2011
claims.quote: a perfectly reliable unreliable narrator

claims.claim: Robinson lists irony, understatement, reticence and sidelong information among the features of Wolfe's style.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', New York Review of Science Fiction, 6 September 2013 (a version introduced The Very Best of Gene Wolfe, PS Publishing, 2011)
claims.quote: irony, understatement, reticence, sidelong information

claims.claim: Robinson names the urge to conceal and to reveal at once as a lasting feature of Wolfe's style.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: the urge both to conceal and to reveal at once

claims.claim: Reading Wolfe's wartime letters home, Robinson says Wolfe wants both to tell and not to tell.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: He wants both to tell and not to tell.

claims.claim: Robinson describes the narrator of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as first-person with a precise, sinuous style.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: a first-person narrator with a precise, sinuous style

claims.claim: Robinson observes that in The Fifth Head of Cerberus the withheld name is accompanied by the telling.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: the not-telling is accompanied by the telling

claims.claim: Robinson says clues in the text point to the withheld family name being canine or lupine.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: clues in the text that the family's last name

claims.claim: Robinson defines the slingshot ending as one in which events accelerate as the narrative nears its end.
claims.source: Kim Stanley Robinson, 'A Story', NYRSF, 6 September 2013
claims.quote: the events begin to speed up as the narrative nears

claims.claim: In an autobiographical essay quoted by Robinson, Wolfe reports his post-war living arrangements and appends the fact that he still dropped to the floor at a loud noise.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, Contemporary Authors Autobiography Series vol. 9, quoted in Kim Stanley Robinson, NYRSF, 2013
claims.quote: still showed a marked tendency to drop to the floor

claims.claim: Mikalatos says Wolfe often places key action scenes off stage.
claims.source: Matt Mikalatos, 'A Brief Introduction to Gene Wolfe, My Favorite Contemporary Author', Speculative Faith / Lorehaven, 15 March 2013
claims.quote: He often has key action scenes take place

claims.claim: Mikalatos says the answers are all present in Wolfe's text but the reader is expected to pay attention.
claims.source: Matt Mikalatos, Speculative Faith / Lorehaven, comment 16 March 2013
claims.quote: The answers are all there, but Wolfe expects you to

claims.claim: A reader reports the device failing for him, saying Wolfe does not seem to want his readers to understand the text.
claims.source: commenter 'shastastwin' on Speculative Faith / Lorehaven, 16 March 2013
claims.quote: He doesn't seem to want his readers to understand the

claims.claim: The same reader contrasts Tolkien, whose surface satisfies alone, with Wolfe, whose surface level he found unsatisfying.
claims.source: commenter 'shastastwin' on Speculative Faith / Lorehaven, 16 March 2013
claims.quote: the surface level of the text is not satisfying

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi observes that Hildegrin is described as bear-like twenty-two chapters before his name or nickname is given.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, 'Lions and Tigers and Bears . . . of the New Sun', Ultan's Library, 28 December 2003
claims.quote: 22 chapters before we are given his name or his

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi reads the Atrium of Time's canted dial and snow-dusted animal statues as an unannounced statement that the world's cycle of seasons is halting.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 28 December 2003
claims.quote: the axis of time is out of alignment

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi notes the threshold guardian of the final combat is never tagged as such in the text.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 28 December 2003
claims.quote: even though as a common mutineer he is not tagged

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi traces an unstated rule across the tetralogy whereby bear-marked foes die and cat-marked ones are spared.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 28 December 2003
claims.quote: the bears are foes who must die, and the cats

claims.claim: A single subordinate clause of Wolfe's, quoted by Andre-Driussi, states the marriage custom of the Bear Tower's beast handlers.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Shadow of the Torturer ch.4 p.41, quoted by Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 2003
claims.quote: each brother takes a lioness or bear-sow in marriage

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi argues the Autarch goes unnamed because the office should be so distant from common people as to be faceless.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, 'The Death of Catherine the Weal and Other Stories', Ultan's Library, posted 27 August 2008 (written 1992)
claims.quote: so distant from the common people as to be faceless

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi argues a name gives an immediate, mystery-dispelling familiarity between ruler and populace or text and reader.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: a name gives an immediate sense of mystery-dispelling familiarity

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi concludes that in the cycle the personal name counts for nothing and the title for everything.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: in the end, the name is nothing, the title

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says it matters to the story that the institutional position of autarch is faceless, nameless and genderless.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: faceless, nameless, and genderless

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi identifies a covert naming rule whereby followers of the New Sun carry saints' names and its enemies carry mythological ones.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: followers of the New Sun are named after saints

claims.claim: Wolfe's own synopsis of the abandoned novella, quoted from The Castle of the Otter, states the premise in flat declarative clauses.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Castle of the Otter, quoted by Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: Severian, an apprentice torturer, meets a lovely prisoner, Thecla, and falls

claims.claim: In Wolfe's own outline the death is reported not as an event but as blood seen seeping under a cell door.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Castle of the Otter, quoted by Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: When he sees blood seeping from under her cell door

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi has to reckon the cycle's chronology in years counted backward from Severian's reign, a scale the text never states outright.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, Ultan's Library, 1992/2008
claims.quote: roughly 20 years PS, or Prior to Severian's reign

claims.claim: Crampton explains that the narrator renders Greek place-names by translating their meanings into his own tongue.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000
claims.quote: Latro attempting to translate the meanings of the Greek words

claims.claim: Crampton points out that the same narrator transliterates people's names rather than translating them, unlike place-names.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000
claims.quote: this is exactly what Latro does with people's names

claims.claim: Crampton argues Wolfe lets a character mistranslate two inscriptions plausibly enough to deceive the reader, in order to stay true to her character.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000
claims.quote: In fact she mistranslates them, but close enough so that

claims.claim: Crampton says the political manoeuvres around the narrator reach the reader only incidentally, because his journal entries stay realistic.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000
claims.quote: we only learn of their importance incidentally

claims.claim: Wolfe's foreword to Soldier of the Mist, quoted by Crampton, says the narrator reports Greece as the Greeks themselves reported it.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, foreword to Soldier of the Mist p.xiii, quoted by Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library
claims.quote: reports Greece as it was reported by the Greeks themselves

claims.claim: Wolfe, in a 1984 interview quoted by Crampton, says a writer should be clear when he wants to be clear and ambiguous when he wishes to be.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Chris Merrick, American Audio Prose Library 1984, quoted by Jeremy Crampton
claims.quote: clear when he wants to be clear

claims.claim: Crampton describes Wolfe's design as a hierarchy letting readers engage at a surface level or a deeper one.
claims.source: Jeremy Crampton, Ultan's Library, 10 August 2000
claims.quote: such complexity is not a disadvantage, but an opportunity

claims.claim: James Gunn, quoted by Crampton, called Wolfe's earlier short fiction usually difficult, often ambiguous and sometimes obscure.
claims.source: James Gunn, Washington Post Book World, 25 May 1980 p.8, quoted by Jeremy Crampton
claims.quote: usually difficult, often ambiguous, sometimes obscure, and always skilfully written

claims.claim: John Clute, quoted by Crampton, says reading Wolfe requires the close critical reading serious critics apply to Modernist novels.
claims.source: John Clute, Strokes (1988) p.159, quoted by Jeremy Crampton
claims.quote: train ourselves in the kind of close critical reading of texts

claims.claim: Wolfe says he learned economy by watching a student editor blue-pencil his story, and understood the editor was removing every word the sentence did not require.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, 'The Wolfe & Gaiman Show', Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: taking out every word the sentence doesn't require

claims.claim: Wolfe says that settling readers' arguments about his books is exactly what he should not do.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: That's exactly what I should not do

claims.claim: Wolfe says there is no sacredness to the text, defending readers who build their own interpretations.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: There's no sacredness to the text

claims.claim: Wolfe explains an unreliable narrator by his occupational type: a man who will not intentionally say anything to his own detriment.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Neil Gaiman, Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: He is not going to tell you intentionally anything

claims.claim: Gaiman says what attracted him and Wolfe to the tourist-guidebook form for their collaboration was its incredibly dry tone.
claims.source: Neil Gaiman in 'The Wolfe & Gaiman Show', Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: the incredibly dry tone

claims.claim: Gaiman describes the guidebook as a form whose style can be taken over and filled with one's own contents.
claims.source: Neil Gaiman in Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: you could take the style and then insert your own

claims.claim: Gaiman says their guidebook borrowed from Charles G. Finney the device of printing a list of the questions the book does not answer.
claims.source: Neil Gaiman in Locus 500, September 2002
claims.quote: the list of unanswered questions

claims.claim: Wolfe states the trick is to leave clues in the story that make an explanation unnecessary.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, 'The Legerdemain of the Wolfe', Thrust: Science Fiction in Review 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: leave clues in the story that make an explanation unnecessary

claims.claim: Wolfe says he always tries to suit the style of the story to its protagonist.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: suit the style of the story to the protagonist

claims.claim: Wolfe says some of his archaic terms were made by stripping Latin words of their endings, mostly for extinct animals.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: made by divesting Latin words of their endings

claims.claim: Wolfe says he used the old spelling Werwolf because it is a valid old spelling that exposes the word's meaning.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: Werwolf is a valid old spelling

claims.claim: Wolfe glosses wergild as the price of a man's life when explaining his naming choices.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: Wergild is the price of a man's life

claims.claim: Wolfe says the inset stories in some instances reveal the character of the teller.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: They reveal the character of the teller, in some instances

claims.claim: Wolfe says an eidetic narrator's advantage is that he can plausibly recount long-past events in detail.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: he can plausibly recount in detail events that took place

claims.claim: Wolfe names as the disadvantage of an eidetic narrator that he cannot plausibly forget.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: he cannot plausibly forget

claims.claim: Wolfe says Severian is fascinated by ideas but is not aware that he is an intellectual and largely lacks the vocabulary.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: he is not aware that he is an intellectual

claims.claim: Wolfe says Severian is a great deal less like most men than he believes himself to be.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: He is a great deal less like most men than

claims.claim: Wolfe stated outright in 1983 that Weer is dead and in spirit reliving his life.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: Weer is dead. In spirit, he is reliving his life

claims.claim: Wolfe says the falling tree at the opening of Peace is what has freed the narrator's ghost.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: It is the fall of that tree

claims.claim: Wolfe says his invented Commonwealth contains a lot of Byzantium and a lot of South America.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: a lot of Byzantium in the Commonwealth, and a lot

claims.claim: Wolfe says that knowing the course of the river Gyoll brings at least ninety per cent of the country with it.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: I know the course of Gyoll; when that is known

claims.claim: Wolfe says he drew a sketch-map of Nessus while writing The Shadow of the Torturer.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe interviewed by Robert Frazier, Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: I made a sketch-map of Nessus

claims.claim: The interviewer describes Wolfe as having planted the truth about Dorcas within the book and concealed it.
claims.source: Robert Frazier, interviewer, in Thrust 19, Winter/Spring 1983
claims.quote: You had planted the truth within the book, and concealed it

claims.claim: Wolfe says anything done in a book must be doing several things at once.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, excerpts from the Locus interview 'Engineering the Future', locusmag.com, 20 March 2011
claims.quote: you really have to be doing several things at once
